checks.Title: Seduce, don't just observe
checks.Evidence: The opening pages establish GLMZ through procedural competence and hardship accounting (suture counts, Φ balances, power-stabilizer failures, antibiotic-strip math) but almost nothing is offered as strange-beautiful or sensuously alluring before the horror of the device/conspiracy lands — the prose states 'The chlorine smell rises, thin and sharp' and 'No ad-glare this deep' as flat facts rather than textures meant to seduce, and the world's wrongness (Nova-7 in the chest, Scalpel, NCID) arrives as plot mechanism, not as something the reader is pulled toward.
checks.Fix: Slow down early on one or two sensory, specific-to-GLMZ images (the orange backup light, the thirty-meter ad-glare line, the Thread's pods drifting like water droplets) and let them do seductive world-building work before the plot's machinery of device/conspiracy takes over, rather than treating the setting mostly as logistical backdrop for competence-porn and exposition.

checks.Title: Open with the world doing its work
checks.Evidence: The opening beats — Jude closing Rudeboi's chest, the failing power stabilizer she 'knows its moods' on, the flat inventory of the Unit's economics, the tray-count ritual — establish a grounded, lived-in world through routine labor before Renata's arrival introduces the plot; the surgery and clinic finances are treated as unremarkable daily grind, exactly the 'stopped being surprised by it' texture the rule asks for.

checks.Title: Gloss first mentions in-voice, never dump
checks.Evidence: Early proprietary terms are glossed cleanly in-voice ('NREN relay — a person-to-person package network, no corpo registry'; 'the Low — the ungoverned band'), but by mid-node dense worldbuilding nouns (Scalpel Division, NCID, Cascade suppressor, GLMZ, Thread's pods, Emergency Provision 7) arrive with thinner or no orientation, e.g. 'the Cascade suppressor rides on his right hip' is explained only via a technical aside about neural mesh rather than a natural first-touch gloss, and 'the Thread's pods hang low' gets zero context at all.
checks.Fix: Give each newly introduced proprietary noun (Scalpel, GLMZ, the Thread) the same one-clause in-voice orientation the early terms get, so a first-time reader isn't left to infer institutional stakes from context alone in the second half.

checks.Title: Never an acronym before its term
checks.Evidence: NREN is used with an immediate gloss ('the NREN relay — a person-to-person package network, no corpo registry') which is fine, but NCID appears first as 'the NCID doesn't take interest below thirty-five' before its expansion 'Halcyon's Neuretic Crime Investigation Division' arrives in the very same sentence only as a trailing clause, and GLMZ is used repeatedly ('the GLMZ medical licensing board', 'GLMZ Wartime Medical Authority', 'Any book could be a reader's first GLMZ book' per the rule) with no full-term expansion anywhere on the page.
checks.Fix: Add an in-voice gloss for GLMZ at its first use (e.g., 'the Greater Lake Michigan Zone's medical licensing board') and restructure the NCID sentence so the full name precedes the acronym rather than trailing it.

checks.Title: Give the POV character one human crack
checks.Evidence: The single closest 'human crack' moment is when Renata says Stash's full name and Stash 'stands one second with the woman's hand loose on the table. One second is all she gives herself for the fact of being known,' immediately re-armoring with 'Then she starts working.' It's present but brief and functional-adjacent; most other emotional beats (the tunnel scene, Femi's fracture backstory, the throat-tightness after the fragment video) are filtered through competence and task-focus rather than a raw personal flash untethered to the plot mechanics.
checks.Fix: Let one of these beats — the named moment, or the throat-tightness watching Renata's video message — linger a sentence longer without pivoting immediately to procedure, so the reader gets an unguarded flicker of Jude as a person before she re-armors.

checks.Title: Land one beat past the handoff
checks.Evidence: The story ends on institutional procedural closure ('She catalogs what she has. She begins.') paired with a wall-mounted memorial name and a pending board hearing — this resolves rather than adds weight; it's a forward-looking bureaucratic status update (license, subpoena, hearing date) followed by a tidy inventory-taking gesture that reads as thematic bookending rather than a single quiet cost-bearing beat.
checks.Fix: Cut the board/hearing exposition paragraph and end instead on one small, wordless physical gesture — Stash's hand on the shelf, or her eyes on the still-warm space where the device used to sit — that carries the cost without narrating the legal machinery forward.

checks.Title: Reward re-reading without requiring it
checks.Evidence: The seemingly throwaway detail that Stash 'has held Nova devices before... but has never seen one in the chest' and her later musing about 412.7 being a dead channel read as pure worldbuilding/procedural texture on a first pass, but on rereading with knowledge of Fragment Six (Renata's direct address explaining she chose Stash for her post-Sable history) these clinical observations retroactively become clues to Renata's eleven-year engineering of this exact encounter — the device warmth 'the way a machine is warm when it has been running,' the anatomically wrong placement 'exactly because it's the last place you'd look,' all pay off differently once the reader knows Renata built this specifically for Stash's hands to find. Similarly, Stash's habitual instrument-counting ritual ('she counts the tray before she has decided to') is introduced as pure characterization but becomes thematically loaded once the reader understands the story's climax turns on completeness versus partial transmission — 'a partial transmission... can be recovered. A full one is complete' — retroactively coloring every earlier counting scene as a rehearsal for the story's central stakes.

checks.Title: Elevate, don't reconstruct
checks.Evidence: The excerpt is a dense, plot-forward thriller sequence (Renata, the device, Scalpel/NCID standoff) built on the same foundational voice and texture established in the opening surgical scenes (Stash's clinical habits, counting instruments, Femi's steadiness) — nothing about the prose suggests a rewrite for newcomers; exposition like the Nova-7 branding, the frequency history, and Stash's Sable backstory is delivered through natural investigative beats (Chit's analyzer, her own memory) rather than inserted signposts, so new readers are onboarded via the same causal chain returning readers would enjoy.
